# 05 HTTP for Backend Engineers

Part of [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/Backend from First Principles|Backend from First Principles]] · Previous: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/04 Benefits of Learning Backend from First Principles/04 Benefits of Learning Backend from First Principles|04 Benefits of Learning Backend from First Principles]] · Next: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/06 Routing/06 Routing|06 Routing]]

**HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the set of rules browsers and servers use to talk to each other: to send data and to receive it. Clients and servers can use other protocols too (WebSocket, gRPC…), but HTTP is one of the most widely used, and almost every backend relies on it.

Backend is a huge field. This series focuses on the parts that show up in most real codebases (roughly 90%), and this lesson covers the HTTP knowledge you need for everyday backend work.

## Contents

1. [[#1. Two core ideas of HTTP|Two core ideas: statelessness and client–server]]
2. [[#2. HTTP, HTTPS, and the network underneath|HTTP, HTTPS, and the network underneath]]
3. [[#3. HTTP versions|HTTP versions]]
4. [[#4. HTTP messages|HTTP messages]]
5. [[#5. Headers|Headers]]
6. [[#6. HTTP methods|HTTP methods]]
7. [[#7. CORS and the OPTIONS method|CORS and the OPTIONS method]]
8. [[#8. Status codes|Status codes]]
9. [[#9. HTTP caching|HTTP caching]]
10. [[#10. Content negotiation|Content negotiation]]
11. [[#11. Compression|Compression]]
12. [[#12. Persistent connections and keep-alive|Persistent connections]]
13. [[#13. Large requests and responses|Large requests and responses]]
14. [[#14. SSL, TLS, and HTTPS|SSL, TLS, and HTTPS]]

---

## 1. Two core ideas of HTTP

### 1.1 Statelessness

**Stateless** means the server has **no memory of past requests**.

- Each request must carry **everything** the server needs to handle it: the URL, the method, headers, and any credentials.
- After the server responds, it **forgets** the request.
- If the same client sends another request, the server treats it as a **brand-new, unrelated** event.

This means requests are **self-contained**.

> **Example:** To view your profile, your browser must send proof of who you are (a cookie or a token) **with every single request**. The server doesn't "remember" that you logged in a minute ago.

**Benefits of being stateless:**

| Benefit | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Simplicity** | The server doesn't have to store session information, which would need extra resources and complexity. |
| **Scalability** | Any server can handle any request, so requests can be spread across many servers. No single server has to "own" a user's session. |
| **Resilience** | If a server crashes, no conversation memory is lost, because there wasn't any to begin with. |

**But apps still need memory sometimes:** staying logged in, keeping items in a shopping cart. Developers add **state management** on top of HTTP using **cookies**, **sessions**, or **tokens**. These come later in the series (lesson 08).

### 1.2 The client–server model

Every HTTP exchange has two sides:

- **Client**: usually a browser or an app. It **starts** the communication by sending a **request**, and must include everything the server needs (the URL, headers, body…).
- **Server**: hosts resources (websites, APIs, files) and **waits** for requests. It processes each one and sends back a **response**: a web page, JSON data, a file, an error message, etc.

> **Rule:** In HTTP, communication is **always started by the client**. The server only ever *responds*.

---

## 2. HTTP, HTTPS, and the network underneath

### HTTP vs HTTPS

For this series, treat **HTTP and HTTPS as interchangeable**. HTTPS is HTTP with extra security (encryption and certificates, through TLS). The underlying ideas are the same. (See [[#14. SSL, TLS, and HTTPS|section 14]].)

### HTTP needs a connection: TCP

Before a client and server can exchange messages, they need a **connection**, a channel to communicate through.

- HTTP itself only requires the transport underneath to be **reliable**: it must not lose messages, or must at least report an error when it does.
- The two most common **transport protocols** on the Internet are:
  - **TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol): connection-based and **reliable**. It makes sure data arrives complete and in order.
  - **UDP** (User Datagram Protocol): faster and simpler, but with no delivery guarantee.
- Because TCP is reliable, traditional HTTP runs on **TCP**.
- TCP opens a connection with a **three-way handshake** (a short "hello / hello back / OK" exchange). That's a networking topic you can explore separately.

### The OSI model and where backend engineers work

The **OSI model** is a common way to describe networking as **7 layers**, from physical cables (layer 1) up to applications (layer 7).

```
7  Application   ← HTTP lives here. Backend engineers mostly work here.
6  Presentation
5  Session
4  Transport     ← TCP / UDP
3  Network       ← IP
2  Data link
1  Physical
```

Topics like the TCP handshake and TLS encryption belong mostly to **network engineering** (the lower layers). They're useful to know, but going deep is a rabbit hole. This series focuses on the **application layer**, with only short notes about the layers below. See also [[Notes/Networking/How the Internet Works|How the Internet Works]].

**What to remember:** the client and server set up a network connection, and then they send and receive **messages**.

---

## 3. HTTP versions

| Version | Key change | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **HTTP/1.0** | A **new TCP connection for every request** | Slow: a connection had to be opened and closed each time. |
| **HTTP/1.1** | **Persistent connections**: many requests and responses reuse one TCP connection. Also added **chunked transfer encoding** and better caching. | Much faster. Still very widely used. |
| **HTTP/2** | **Multiplexing**: many requests and responses at the same time over one connection. Uses **binary framing** instead of plain text, **header compression** (HPACK), and **server push** (the server sends resources before they're asked for). | More efficient use of a single connection. |
| **HTTP/3** | Built on **QUIC**, a transport protocol that runs on **UDP** instead of TCP. | Faster connection setup, lower latency, better handling of lost packets, and multiplexing **without head-of-line blocking**. |

**Head-of-line blocking** = when one slow or lost piece of data holds up everything queued behind it. HTTP/2 still suffers from this at the TCP level; HTTP/3 avoids it.

Again, this is networking detail. The takeaway: **a connection is made, and messages flow over it.**

---

## 4. HTTP messages

There are two kinds of HTTP message:

- **Request**: sent by the client to the server.
- **Response**: sent by the server back to the client.

### A request message (example)

```http
POST /api/notes HTTP/1.1                  ← request line: method, resource URL, HTTP version
Host: api.example.com                     ← headers (key: value pairs)
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Length: 39
                                          ← blank line = "headers are over"
{"title": "Groceries", "body": "milk"}    ← request body
```

| Part | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Method** (`POST`) | What kind of action the client wants. |
| **Resource URL** (`/api/notes`) | Which resource on the server. |
| **HTTP version** (`HTTP/1.1`) | Which version of the protocol is in use. |
| **Host** header | The domain of the server being contacted. |
| **Other headers** | Extra information (metadata) about the request. |
| **Blank line** | Marks the end of the headers. |
| **Body** | The data the client is sending to the server. |

### A response message (example)

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created                      ← status line: version, status code, status text
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 52
Date: Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:00:00 GMT
                                          ← blank line
{"id": 17, "title": "Groceries", "body": "milk"}   ← response body
```

- **Status code** (`201`) + **status text** (`Created`): the result of the request.
- Then **response headers**, a **blank line**, and the **response body**.

(These are illustrative messages, not output captured from the lesson's demo.)

---

## 5. Headers

### What are headers?

Headers are **key–value pairs** of extra information (**metadata**) sent with a request or response, e.g. `Content-Type: application/json`.

### Why have a separate section for them?

Why not put everything into the URL or the body? Think about **sending a parcel**:

- The recipient's name, address, postcode, and phone number are written **on the outside** of the package.
- Everyone who handles it along the way can read the information they need **without opening it**.
- If that information were inside, every handler would have to open the parcel just to see where it goes.

HTTP headers work the same way. The **body** is the contents; the **headers** are the label. Servers, proxies, and browsers can read headers quickly to decide how to handle the message, without digging into the body. Headers have other uses too, covered below.

### Categories of headers

#### 1. Request headers

Sent by the client to describe **the client and what it wants**. They help the server understand the client's environment, preferences, and capabilities.

| Header | Purpose | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `User-Agent` | What kind of client is sending the request (browser, Postman, a server, a mobile app) | `User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 ...` |
| `Authorization` | Credentials to identify the user, e.g. a **bearer token** | `Authorization: Bearer abc123` |
| `Accept` | What content types the client wants back | `Accept: application/json` |

#### 2. General headers

Used in **both** requests and responses; they describe the **message itself**.

| Header | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `Date` | When the message was created |
| `Cache-Control` | Caching rules, e.g. `no-cache`, `max-age=60` |
| `Connection` | Keep the connection open (`keep-alive`) or close it (`close`) |

#### 3. Representation headers

Describe the **body** (the "representation" of the resource), so the receiver knows how to read it.

| Header | Purpose | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Content-Type` | The **media type** (format) of the body | `application/json`, `text/html` |
| `Content-Length` | Size of the body in **bytes** | `Content-Length: 348` |
| `Content-Encoding` | Any compression applied | `gzip`, `deflate` |
| `ETag` | A unique identifier for a version of the resource, mostly used for caching | `ETag: "a1b2c3"` |

#### 4. Security headers

Control browser behavior to **protect** the client and server from attacks.

| Header | What it does | Attack it helps prevent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Strict-Transport-Security` (**HSTS**) | Forces the browser to use **HTTPS only** for this site | **Protocol downgrade** attacks (forcing a connection back to insecure HTTP) |
| `Content-Security-Policy` (**CSP**) | Limits where scripts, styles, images, etc. can be loaded from | **Cross-site scripting (XSS)**: injecting malicious scripts into a page |
| `X-Frame-Options` | Stops the page from being shown inside an `<iframe>` on another site | **Clickjacking**: tricking users into clicking hidden elements |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | Tells the browser **not to guess** the content type | **MIME-type sniffing** attacks |
| `Set-Cookie` with `HttpOnly` / `Secure` | `HttpOnly`: JavaScript can't read the cookie. `Secure`: the cookie is only sent over HTTPS | Cookie theft |

**MIME type** = the official name for a content format, like `text/html` or `image/png`.

### Two big ideas behind headers

#### Extensibility

HTTP is **highly extensible** (easy to extend): you can add new headers **without changing the protocol itself**. Just adding some metadata can change how the whole interaction behaves. This lets HTTP adapt to new needs:

- **Security improvements**: e.g. `Strict-Transport-Security` was added to force secure connections.
- **Custom headers**: developers can invent their own for their app, e.g. `X-Custom-Header`.
- **Content negotiation**: `Accept`, `Accept-Language`, and `Accept-Encoding` let servers send different versions of content depending on what the client prefers.

#### Headers as a "remote control"

Headers let the **client send instructions or preferences** that change how the server responds:

- **Content negotiation**: `Accept: text/html` → the server sends HTML; `Accept: application/json` → it sends JSON.
- **Caching control**: the server uses `Cache-Control` or `Expires` to say how long the client may cache a response.
- **Authentication**: the client proves who it is with the `Authorization` header, which affects what it's allowed to access.

---

## 6. HTTP methods

Methods exist to express the **intent** of a request: what kind of action the client wants. Instead of every request meaning the same thing, the method gives each one a clear **semantic meaning** (agreed-upon meaning).

| Method | Intent | Has a body? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | **Fetch** data. Must **not** change anything on the server. | No |
| `POST` | **Create** something new on the server | Yes (the data to create) |
| `PATCH` | **Update part** of a resource, e.g. change only the user's name | Yes |
| `PUT` | **Replace** a resource completely with the data sent | Yes |
| `DELETE` | **Remove** a resource | Usually no |

### PATCH vs PUT

- **PATCH** = a **selective** update. Only the fields you send change.
- **PUT** = a **complete replacement**. Whatever you send becomes the whole new resource.

```text
Existing user:  { "name": "Ana", "email": "ana@x.com", "age": 30 }

PATCH { "name": "Anna" }
→ { "name": "Anna", "email": "ana@x.com", "age": 30 }   (only name changed)

PUT { "name": "Anna" }
→ { "name": "Anna" }                                     (everything replaced)
```

Developers often use PUT when they really mean PATCH, which goes against the semantics. **The creator's rule of thumb:** use **PATCH** unless you have a specific reason to replace the whole resource.

### Idempotent vs non-idempotent

An **idempotent** method can be repeated many times and the **result on the server is the same** as doing it once.

| Method | Idempotent? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | ✅ Yes | Fetching data doesn't change it, however many times you do it. |
| `PUT` | ✅ Yes | Replacing a resource with the same data again gives the same result. |
| `DELETE` | ✅ Yes | Once a resource is deleted, it stays deleted. Deleting it again doesn't change the outcome. |
| `POST` | ❌ No | Each request creates something **new**. |

> **Example (POST):** A user creates a note. The first POST creates note #1. Sending the exact same POST again creates note #2. Same request, different results → **non-idempotent**.

(For DELETE, a second call may *respond* differently, e.g. with 404 Not Found, but the **state of the server** is the same: the resource is gone.)

### OPTIONS

There's one more method, **`OPTIONS`**, which asks the server **what it supports**. You'll rarely send it yourself, but you'll see it in the browser's Network tab as part of **CORS preflight requests** (next section).

---

## 7. CORS and the OPTIONS method

See also: [[Notes/Web Development/CORS|CORS]] and [[Notes/Web Development/Same-Origin Policy|Same-Origin Policy]].

### The background: the same-origin policy

An **origin** = scheme + domain + port, e.g. `https://example.com:443`.

By default, browsers follow the **same-origin policy**: JavaScript on a web page may only make requests to the **same origin** that served the page. A request to a different origin (e.g. from `example.com` to `api.another-example.com`) is a **cross-origin** request, and the browser blocks access to the response unless the server allows it.

**CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the mechanism that lets a server say **who may access its resources, and how**. It is enforced by the **browser**.

There are two CORS flows: **simple requests** and **preflighted requests**.

### 7.1 Simple request flow

Setup: frontend at `example.com`, API at `api.example.com`. The frontend makes a `GET` request.

```
Browser (page on example.com)                    Server (api.example.com)
   │  GET /data                                        │
   │  Origin: https://example.com   ← added by browser │
   │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────►│
   │                                                   │ checks Origin against its CORS policy
   │  200 OK                                           │
   │  Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://example.com │
   │ ◄─────────────────────────────────────────────────│
   │ Browser checks the header → match → lets JS read the response
```

1. The browser automatically adds an **`Origin`** header saying where the request comes from.
2. The request uses a **simple method**: `GET`, `POST`, or `HEAD`.
3. The server compares `Origin` with its CORS policy.
4. If the origin is allowed, the server adds **`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`** to the response, with either:
   - the client's origin (e.g. `https://example.com`), or
   - `*`, meaning **any origin is allowed**.
5. The browser sees the request was cross-origin and checks for that header. If it matches, the response is passed to the JavaScript code.

**If the server doesn't allow the origin**, it leaves out `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. The browser notices the header is missing, **blocks** the response, and shows a **CORS error** in the console and the Network tab.

### 7.2 Preflighted request flow

For some requests, the browser first sends a **preflight request**: an extra request **before** the real one, asking the server whether the real request is allowed.

**When does a request need a preflight?** It must be **cross-origin**, and **at least one** of these must be true:

1. The method is **not** `GET`, `POST`, or `HEAD` (e.g. `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`).
2. The request includes **non-simple headers**. Only a small list of headers count as "simple" (CORS-safelisted, such as `Accept` or `Content-Language`); anything else, like `Authorization` or a custom `X-...` header, triggers a preflight.
3. The **`Content-Type`** of the request is something **other than**:
   - `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
   - `multipart/form-data`
   - `text/plain`

Most modern APIs send **JSON** bodies (`Content-Type: application/json`), so **most cross-origin API requests are preflighted**.

**The preflight request** uses the **OPTIONS** method and has **no body**. It's just a question about the server's capabilities:

```http
OPTIONS /api/notes/17 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Origin: https://example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT                ← "Do you allow PUT on this URL?"
Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization     ← "Do you allow this header?"
```

**If the server supports CORS**, it answers:

```http
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://example.com      ← this origin is allowed (or *)
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PUT, DELETE             ← these methods are allowed
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization           ← this header is allowed
Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400                         ← cache this answer for 24 hours
```

| Response header | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `204 No Content` | Success, with no body. All the information is in the headers. |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | The origin is allowed (or `*` for all). |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` | Methods allowed for this route. |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` | Non-simple headers allowed. |
| `Access-Control-Max-Age` | How long (in seconds) the browser may **reuse** this answer instead of sending another preflight. Saves bandwidth for both sides. |

The browser checks each item. If everything is allowed, it sends the **real request** (e.g. the `PUT` with its body), and the server responds normally. If the server doesn't handle CORS, it won't send these headers, and the browser **blocks** the request.

**Simple flow + preflight flow together = the full CORS flow.**

### 7.3 What the demo showed

The demos used **Burp Suite**, a tool used by security testers ("ethical hackers"), to **intercept and view HTTP traffic**. The lesson deliberately shows **no server code**: the concepts are the same in any language or framework.

Setup: frontend at `localhost:5173`, API on a different port of `localhost` (e.g. `localhost:3000`). Even on the same machine, **a different port means a different origin**, so the browser treats these requests as cross-origin.

- **Simple request:** the request had `Origin: http://localhost:5173`. The response included `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with that origin, so the data rendered on the page.
- **Same request, header removed on the server:** the browser **blocked** the response and showed a **CORS error**.
- **Preflighted request:** a `PUT` with an `Authorization` header and a JSON body (all three preflight conditions; any one would have been enough).
  1. First, an `OPTIONS` request with `Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT` and a request for the `Authorization` and `Content-Type` headers.
  2. The server responded `204 No Content` with `Allow-Origin` (the frontend's origin), `Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE`, `Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization`, and `Max-Age: 0` (set to zero only for testing, so a preflight would fire every time).
  3. Then the real `PUT` request went through with its body, and got a normal response.

---

## 8. Status codes

### Why status codes exist

A **status code** tells the client the **result** of its request in a **standard** way.

- The client doesn't have to guess from the body ("if it worked I'd expect this structure; if the server crashed I'd get null…"). One number tells it.
- Clients can **react** to specific codes:
  - `401` → log the user out and ask them to log in again.
  - `400` → ask the user to fix the form and resubmit.
- They're **standardized**: whether your server is written in Python, Go, Rust, JavaScript, or Ruby, you follow the same codes (e.g. `200` for success, `201` for "created").

Before status codes were standardized, clients had to guess the outcome from the response content, which was inconsistent and inefficient.

### The five classes

Status codes are **three-digit numbers**. The **first digit** gives the category:

| Range | Category |
| --- | --- |
| **1xx** | Informational |
| **2xx** | Success |
| **3xx** | Redirection |
| **4xx** | Client error (the request has a problem) |
| **5xx** | Server error (the server has a problem) |

### 1xx: Informational (rarely used day to day)

| Code | Meaning | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **100 Continue** | "I got your headers; go ahead and send the body." | Large uploads: the client sends headers first and only sends the big body if the server agrees. |
| **101 Switching Protocols** | The server is switching protocols as the client asked. | Upgrading from HTTP to **WebSocket**. |

### 2xx: Success

| Code | Meaning | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **200 OK** | Success. Here's the resource / the action was done. | A successful `GET` |
| **201 Created** | Success, and a **new resource was created**. | A successful `POST` or form submission |
| **204 No Content** | Success, but there's **no body** to return. | CORS preflight responses; sometimes `DELETE` |

### 3xx: Redirection

| Code | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **301 Moved Permanently** | The resource has a **new URL for good**; use it from now on. | You rename `/user` to `/person`. To keep old apps working (**backward compatibility**), `/user` returns 301 → `/person`. |
| **302 Found** (temporary redirect) | The resource is **temporarily** somewhere else; keep using the original URL in future. | During a few-hour campaign, you redirect a route to a special page, then switch it back. |
| **304 Not Modified** | The resource **hasn't changed** since you last fetched it; use your cached copy. | Used with **conditional GET** requests and ETags (see [[#9. HTTP caching|caching]]). |

### 4xx: Client errors

As a backend engineer you'll deal with these most often: they're caused by something about the **client's request**.

| Code | Meaning | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **400 Bad Request** | The request data is invalid. | You expect a number and get an array or string; you expect an email and get a phone number. "Fix your request and try again." |
| **401 Unauthorized** | **Not authenticated**: credentials are missing, invalid, or expired. | The client sent no JWT token, or the token expired. |
| **403 Forbidden** | **Authenticated, but not allowed** to do this. | User A tries to delete User B's resource. |
| **404 Not Found** | The resource doesn't exist. | Wrong URL, or the resource was deleted. |
| **405 Method Not Allowed** | Wrong HTTP method for this route. | Sending `PUT` to a route that only accepts `GET`/`POST`, often a typo on the frontend (e.g. PATCH instead of PUT). |
| **409 Conflict** | The request conflicts with the current state. | Folder names must be unique; the user tries to create a folder whose name already exists. |
| **429 Too Many Requests** | **Rate limit** exceeded. | Your server allows, say, at most 60 requests per second per client; the client goes over that. |

**401 vs 403**, the classic confusion:

- **401**: "I don't know **who you are**." (Not authenticated.)
- **403**: "I know who you are, but you're **not allowed**." (Not authorized.)

### 5xx: Server errors

| Code | Meaning | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **500 Internal Server Error** | Something unexpected broke on the server. | An unhandled exception. Better than returning nothing or leaving the request hanging. |
| **501 Not Implemented** | The server doesn't support this method or feature (yet). | A feature is planned but not built. |
| **502 Bad Gateway** | A **proxy** got an **invalid response** from the server behind it (the **upstream** server). | Usually produced by proxies or load balancers like Nginx, not by your code. |
| **503 Service Unavailable** | The server is **temporarily** unable to handle requests. | Too much traffic, or maintenance. "Try again later." |
| **504 Gateway Timeout** | A proxy got **no response in time** from the upstream server. | Nginx waited for your app and gave up. |

**Upstream server** = the server *behind* a proxy that does the real work (e.g. your Node app behind Nginx, as in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/03 What Is a Backend/03 What Is a Backend|lesson 03]]).

These cover roughly 95% of what you'll need.

### What the demo showed

A demo frontend fired requests at a mock server set up to return each code. Every real request was preceded by an `OPTIONS` preflight, because they were cross-origin. Results: `200 OK`; `201 Created` ("resource created successfully"); `400 Bad Request` ("missing required data"); `401 Unauthorized`; `403 Forbidden`; `404 Not Found`; `409 Conflict` ("resource already exists"); `500 Internal Server Error`; `503 Service Unavailable` ("please try again later").

Note that the 500 response just said "Internal server error". It deliberately didn't reveal details to the client, **for security reasons**.

---

## 9. HTTP caching

**HTTP caching** stores copies of responses so they can be **reused** instead of downloaded again. This means:

- **faster** load times,
- **less bandwidth**: the client downloads less and the server sends less,
- **less server load**.

The core idea: **if the data hasn't changed, reuse the old copy.**

### The three key response headers

| Header | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Cache-Control: max-age=10` | You may keep using this response for up to **10 seconds** without asking again. |
| `ETag: "3141"` | An identifier for **this version** of the resource. Usually a **hash** (a short fingerprint calculated from the content). The demo used a random number for simplicity. |
| `Last-Modified: <date>` | When the resource last changed. |

### The two key request headers (conditional GET)

When the browser has a cached copy, it asks: "**only send it again if it changed**":

| Header | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `If-None-Match: "3141"` | Send a new version only if the current ETag is **different** from this one. |
| `If-Modified-Since: <date>` | Send a new version only if it changed **after** this date. |

### The flow (as shown in the demo)

```
1) First GET /api/resource
   ← 200 OK, body, Cache-Control: max-age=10, ETag: "3141", Last-Modified: T1

2) GET again, with If-None-Match: "3141", If-Modified-Since: T1
   ← 304 Not Modified (no body) → browser reuses its cached copy

3) Client updates the resource (the demo used POST; PATCH/PUT would be more correct)
   ← 200 OK, new ETag: "2943"

4) GET with the OLD ETag "3141"
   ← 200 OK, new body, ETag: "2943"   (it changed, so a fresh copy is sent)

5) GET with If-None-Match: "2943"
   ← 304 Not Modified   (this is the latest version)
```

### Limitations, and the creator's opinion

In production, HTTP caching gets complicated: the server must generate and manage ETags correctly. If it **forgets to update an ETag**, clients keep using an **outdated** cached copy.

The creator prefers **client-side caching libraries** such as **React Query**, where the client decides when to use the cache and when to refetch (e.g. on a set interval). In their opinion this is often better than traditional HTTP caching, which is still a good option for **simple** use cases.

## 10. Content negotiation

**Content negotiation** is how the client and server **agree on the best format** for the data. The client states its preferences; the server responds in a matching format, or a **fallback** if it can't.

| Type | Request header | Example values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Media type** (format) | `Accept` | `application/json`, `application/xml`, `text/html` |
| **Language** | `Accept-Language` | `en` (English), `es` (Spanish) |
| **Encoding** (compression) | `Accept-Encoding` | `gzip`, `deflate`, `br` (Brotli), `zstd` |

### What the demo showed

1. **Default:** `Accept-Language: en`, `Accept: application/json`, `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd` (sent by the browser) → **JSON in English**.
2. **Language changed to Spanish** (`Accept-Language: es`) → **JSON in Spanish**.
3. **Format changed to XML** (`Accept: application/xml`) → **XML in Spanish**.

The client says what it prefers; the server adapts. This makes life easier for clients.

---

## 11. Compression

**HTTP compression** is part of content negotiation: the client lists the encodings it supports in `Accept-Encoding`, and the server compresses the body with one of them, saying which in **`Content-Encoding`**. The browser **decompresses** it automatically and gets the original data.

Common formats: **gzip**, **deflate**, **br** (Brotli).

### What the demo showed

A response with a large JSON file (about 11,000 entries):

| Compression | Transferred size |
| --- | --- |
| **On** (`Content-Encoding: gzip`) | about **3.8 MB** |
| **Off** | about **26 MB** |

Same data, roughly **7× larger** without compression. Imagine every client downloading 26 MB: a huge waste of bandwidth. That's why large responses should be compressed.

---

## 12. Persistent connections and keep-alive

This mostly works **behind the scenes**. The defaults are usually fine, but it's good to know.

- **HTTP/1.0:** every request–response needed its **own TCP connection**. Opening and closing TCP connections is slow and resource-heavy.
- **HTTP/1.1:** introduced **persistent connections**, so one TCP connection is **reused** for many requests and responses. This lowers latency and saves resources.

Key points:

1. **In HTTP/1.1, connections are persistent by default.** They stay open unless explicitly closed. You don't have to do anything.
2. **`Connection: keep-alive`** can still be sent to explicitly ask the server to keep the connection open. A related `Keep-Alive` header can set options:
   - `timeout`: how long to keep the idle connection open,
   - `max`: how many requests may use it before it closes.
3. **`Connection: close`** closes the connection after the response. This was HTTP/1.0's default behavior, and it can still be forced in HTTP/1.1.

## 13. Large requests and responses

### Sending large files to the server: multipart requests

For uploading files (images, video, audio…), clients use **multipart** requests: the data is sent in **parts** instead of as one JSON body.

```http
POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryABC123
Content-Length: 204800

------WebKitFormBoundaryABC123
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="photo.jpg"
Content-Type: image/jpeg

<binary data of the image...>
------WebKitFormBoundaryABC123--
```

- **`Content-Type: multipart/form-data`** says the body is made of parts.
- **`boundary=...`** defines the **delimiter**: a unique string that **separates the parts**. In the demo, searching the body showed the boundary at the **start** of the binary data and again at the **end**.
- The server reads the file and responds with some details about it to confirm the upload worked.

**Rule:** when sending large files to a server, use **multipart** requests.

### Sending large data to the client: streaming in chunks

The demo streamed a large text file from server to client **in chunks** instead of all at once.

Important response headers:

| Header | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Content-Type: text/event-stream` | The data will arrive as a **stream of events** (pieces), not a single text body. |
| `Connection: keep-alive` | Keep the connection open until all the data has been sent. |

The client kept receiving chunks and **appending** them, gradually rebuilding the whole file. This is how a server can send large responses using **chunked transfer** / **event streams**.

## 14. SSL, TLS, and HTTPS

You rarely work with these directly at the application level, but you should know what they are.

| Term | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **SSL** (Secure Sockets Layer) | The **original** protocol for encrypting communication between client and server, so passwords and card numbers can't be read by attackers. Now **outdated** because of security vulnerabilities. |
| **TLS** (Transport Layer Security) | The **modern, more secure replacement** for SSL. It **encrypts data in transit** (protecting it from being intercepted or tampered with) and uses **certificates** to **authenticate the server** (prove it's really who it claims to be). It's updated over time; the current recommended version is **TLS 1.3**. |
| **HTTPS** | **HTTP + TLS**. When you visit an `https://` site, TLS encrypts everything between your browser and the server, protecting things like login credentials. |

**Eavesdropping** = secretly listening to communication. TLS prevents it.

## Key takeaways

- HTTP is **stateless** (each request is self-contained) and **client–server** (the client always starts).
- Traditional HTTP runs on **TCP**; HTTP/3 runs on **QUIC over UDP**. Backend engineers mostly work at the **application layer**.
- A message = start line + **headers** + blank line + **body**. Headers are metadata, like the label on a parcel.
- Header categories: **request**, **general**, **representation**, **security**. Headers make HTTP **extensible** and act like a **remote control**.
- Methods express **intent**. GET, PUT, and DELETE are **idempotent**; POST is not. Prefer **PATCH** for partial updates.
- **CORS**: browsers block cross-origin responses unless the server sends `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers. Non-simple requests trigger an **OPTIONS preflight**.
- **Status codes** give a standard result: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
- **Caching** uses `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified` → `If-None-Match` / `If-Modified-Since` → `304 Not Modified`.
- **Content negotiation** (`Accept`, `Accept-Language`, `Accept-Encoding`) and **compression** (gzip, br) shape the response.
- Use **multipart** for uploads, **streaming** for large responses, and **HTTPS (TLS)** for security.
